articles.title: JENNIFER GRIFFIN: I covered wars, terror and tragedy for Fox News. What I found was a family
articles.summary: Fox News' Jennifer Griffin recalls covering Vladimir Putin's rise in Moscow, the Kosovo War and the Second Intifada across nearly three decades.
articles.body: I started reporting for Fox News in 1997, shortly after its launch in October 1996, while based in Moscow. Russian President Boris Yeltsin had just undergone heart surgery in November when I arrived, and the Mir Space Station, a Soviet-Russian station, with American astronauts on board, caught fire — the first fire on an international space station. Every Monday, Yeltsin seemed to fire his cabinet, sending shock waves through the Western world. Vladimir Putin had moved to Moscow in 1996. In March 1997, Yeltsin appointed him deputy chief of the Presidential Staff and chief of the Main Control Directorate to work as an auditor in the Kremlin and to get close to Yeltsin. He later took over as head of the FSB, the successor to the KGB, and staged what independent critics, intelligence officials, and dissidents long alleged were a series of false flag operations that involved blowing up four apartment buildings filled with women and children sleeping in their beds to justify an invasion of Chechnya. During that time, in Moscow and St. Petersburg, bankers were gunned down, their bodies found in the streets as the ruble crashed and the rising Russian mafia and oligarchs began dividing up Russian state enterprises and assets. FOX NEWS' JENNIFER GRIFFIN AWARDED 2024 PRIZE OF PROFESSIONAL EXCELLENCE AT THE FOREIGN PRESS AWARDS After starting with Fox in 1997, I remember standing on an icy-cold bridge on New Year’s Eve with the snow at times blowing upwards over the Moskva River and St. Basil’s onion dome cathedral lit up in the background as drunken Russians careened toward our camera position and fireworks lit the midnight sky over the Kremlin. I was learning on the job how to do stand-up and live shots for this new American cable television network, which hoped to compete with CNN. I was working for Simon Marks, a former ITN correspondent, who hired me as the Fox News correspondent in Moscow to work for Feature Story Productions, which had a contract to provide coverage for the new channel. I was trained in print and radio, not television. I had to learn on the job. Soon I was assigned by Fox to cover the Kosovo War from NATO headquarters in Brussels during its bombing campaign in March 1999. Gen. Wesley Clark was NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander, and I will never forget the mood at NATO headquarters when a U.S. B-2 Spirit dropped five satellite-guided bombs (JDAMs) on the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade, killing three Chinese journalists and injuring dozens. MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME The mistake was the result of a CIA miscalculation of coordinates associated with the intended target: a Yugoslav weapons storage facility. Months later, after the Serbs were forced to withdraw, I flew to Kosovo, joining Fox’s Greg Palkot on the ground. We took over from David Lee Miller and the Jerusalem team, including Yaniv Turgeman and Eli Fastman, who had remained in Belgrade during the NATO bombing campaign. We divided up shifts, and I talked my way into a Russian base by offering cigarettes to a Russian soldier after the Russians surprised the U.S. military by landing in the Kosovo capital. I talked my way onto an American Black Hawk helicopter that was delivering 82nd Airborne troops to observe the Serbian soldiers withdrawing. We got the footage of the withdrawal and dashed back to make it on air for "Fox Report." I remember our cameraman, Mal James, lifting his camera to shoot the arrival of the Apache helicopters above Pristina with their nose-mounted sensors and night vision. I spoke into the microphone with the new Fox mic flag: "Here come the Apaches!" They were a fierce symbol of American technology and air supremacy. Fast-forward to the end of 1999. Fox hired me full time as its Jerusalem correspondent. My husband and I moved from Moscow. It was the tail end of the Oslo Peace Accords, which were on life support. President Clinton was trying to rescue them before leaving office by meeting frequently with Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Palestinian Chairman Yasser Arafat. DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE We thought this would be our most boring assignment after having lived in South Africa at the end of apartheid, Islamabad as the Taliban were being formed, and Kabul amid the civil war among the Mujahideen. We decided to start our family. Months later, on September 28, 2000, Ariel Sharon, who had served as Israel’s defense minister and was challenging Bibi Netanyahu as the leader of the Likud Party, decided to take a walk up to the Temple Mount. I had just found out I was pregnant and had morning sickness as I covered the first rocks being thrown down onto Jews praying at the Western Wall. Friday prayers erupted at the Haram al-Sharif. There was tear gas and injured Palestinians were taken away on stretchers. The Second Intifada began and lasted for the next seven-and-a-half years while I was posted in Jerusalem. I had two daughters born in Jerusalem during that time, when my Fox team and I responded to every suicide bombing, every incursion into the West Bank and Gaza. JUAN WILLIAMS: MY WIFE THOUGHT I WAS CRAZY TO JOIN FOX NEWS. I'M GLAD I DID I wore a flak jacket and remember where I was at an Israeli checkpoint in Ramallah in the West Bank, doing a stand-up, when the first plane slammed into a World Trade Center tower on 9/11. That night, I reported outside our Jerusalem bureau for Fox’s "America’s Most Wanted" to talk about the likely suspects, including Osama bin Laden. I profiled the shadowy Hezbollah military commander Imad Mughniyah, who had until that point had the blood of more Americans on his hands than any other terrorist following his role in the Marine barracks bombing in Beirut. Our bureau chief was Uri Dan, who wrote for years for the New York Post and had started as a defense reporter in the Yom Kippur War. Eli Fastman ran the bureau and deployed our cameras, producers and correspondents. DR. MARC SIEGEL: WHAT 18 YEARS AT FOX TAUGHT ME ABOUT COURAGE AND FAITH Soon, as the Intifada wore on, more Fox correspondents and anchors came to help with our coverage. In those days and since, we were part of a family. There was not the usual competition among reporters that you might find at other television networks. We were young, scrappy, often outgunned, but we liked to compete from the get-go, even with limited resources and fewer teams. We beat the competition often through ingenuity, contacts and gutsy camera crews. There was plenty of work to go around, and everyone got plenty of airtime. I covered the siege of Bethlehem with Geraldo when armed Palestinian gunmen holed up in the Church of the Nativity and conducted the first interviews in Tulkarm with the Al-Aqsa Martyrs Brigades, a new armed wing linked to the Palestinian Authority that competed with Hamas. Palestinian politician Marwan Barghouti was believed to be helping distribute weapons. I interviewed him before he was arrested and sent to an Israeli prison, where he remains today, 24 years later. I had one of the last interviews with the wheelchair-bound Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, the founder and spiritual leader of Hamas, before he was killed by an Israeli missile as he left a mosque. I covered Yasser Arafat’s funeral from a rooftop in Ramallah as his coffin was tossed in the air above the heads of a sea of Palestinians. FOX NEWS MEDIA'S SPOTLIGHT AWARDS CELEBRATE BEHIND-THE-SCENES STARS AS NETWORK NEARS 30 YEARS The day after Christmas in 2004, with two young children still surrounded by wrapping paper and toys, I was sent by Fox to cover the tsunami, the worst natural disaster to ever hit Thailand and Indonesia. More than 200,000 people were dead after waves up to 100 feet high hit the coasts of 14 countries. My Israeli team and I arrived quickly because there was a direct flight to Phuket from Tel Aviv. We took motorcycles up the coast to get to the epicenter of the damage in Khao Lak, north of Phuket. There were still bodies in the trees, thrown there by the wave, and bloated corpses rotting in the sun. It was an emotional rollercoaster as we reported and searched the temples where bodies were stacked like cordwood. That New Year’s Eve, I broke down on air as I stood in front of the endless photos of the missing, an image that until that point had been a symbol of those lost during 9/11. Later, I reported live from the living rooms of settlers being pulled from their homes by young Israeli soldiers with tears running down their faces during the withdrawal from 21 Jewish settlements in Gaza ordered by Prime Minister Sharon in 2005. It was an early use of LiveU technology, which eventually transformed where we could report live — giving us the ability to take our viewers into the middle of some of the most explosive news stories of the last 20 years. WATCH: FOX NEWS CELEBRATES 30 YEARS OF HEADLINES, DEBATES, LAUGHS AND MORE Fast-forward to the summer of 2006 and the 34-day war between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon after Hezbollah ambushed and kidnapped several Israeli soldiers along the northern border. I stood on a rooftop with Shepard Smith and his team, including our now-president of Fox News, Jay Wallace, as Katyusha rockets flew over the border into northern Israel. There is a photo of us reporting live and ducking from the incoming rockets during one particularly heavy volley. At dawn, after the ceasefire was declared, we got a call from Gaza that our Fox colleagues Steve Centanni and Olaf Wiig had been kidnapped by an armed Palestinian faction. Rather than going home from Kiryat Shmona, Eli Fastman and I drove straight to Gaza. Olaf’s then-wife, Anita McKnight, joined us a day later, along with an executive from Fox. We pounded the pavement and met with every wanted Palestinian militia commander and Hamas leader to seek their release. The clan who kidnapped them was affiliated with a shadowy criminal, Mumtaz Daghmoush. They made videos of our colleagues that looked like the videos ISIS made before beheading other journalists. Fox used every resource at its disposal to get our colleagues released safely — and they were — after two terrifying weeks. After that, I decided it was time for my family and me to return to the United States. The dangers and the exhaustion from covering the Middle East were mounting. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Fox assigned me to the Pentagon, where I have served as national security correspondent since 2007. I arrived with Defense Secretary Robert Gates as Gen. David Petraeus took over in Iraq and began "the surge." I had hoped to stay out of the Middle East for a while, but within a month I was flying to Baghdad. I have covered eight defense secretaries during my time at the Pentagon. I flew all over the world on the E-4B Doomsday plane, the Cold War-era plane capable of conducting a war during a nuclear strike, with nearly all of these Pentagon chiefs. I have spent the past 19 years covering the Pentagon and the U.S. military for Fox, and it has been the honor of a lifetime. Fox is family, and as we look back over these past 30 years, I am proud to work at a place where many of those who started when the network was launched are still putting the news on the air each day. I have had the same voices in my ear since those early days. I have had wonderful producers — Liz Friden, Lucas Tomlinson, Serafin Gomez, Justin Fishel, Yonat Friling and Yael Kuriel, to name a few — who became close friends. I will never forget their kindness, and I will always be grateful for being given a front-row seat to witness history. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM JENNIFER GRIFFIN

articles.title: 'Story matters, so does how you get it': Delhi Police lays down rules for scribes covering protests
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police on Monday issued an advisory for journalists covering protests, asking them to carry valid identity cards and ensure that their
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police on Monday issued an advisory for journalists covering protests, asking them to carry valid identity cards and ensure that their presence or activities do not obstruct police operations or the movement of law enforcement personnel.In a social media post on X, Delhi Police issued the guidelines for journalists and said, "The story matters, so does how you get it!""All journalists assigned to cover protests are advised to carry valid identity cards issued by their respective organisations and/or valid PIB/DIP accreditation cards," the guidelines read."They should keep their identification cards visibly displayed at all times to facilitate identification by law enforcement agencies present at the site. They should also ensure that their presence or activities do not obstruct police operations or the movement of law enforcement personnel," it added."During tense situations, journalists present at the site should maintain a reasonable and safe distance while covering and recording the proceedings. They should position themselves in a manner that clearly distinguishes them from protestors," it further said.This comes days after three women journalists accused Delhi Police officers of sexual harassment during Saturday's protest against the Election Commission at Jantar Mantar.Delhi Police received the complaints and forwarded them to the Crime Branch for further inquiry.On Sunday, Delhi Police, on its official X handle, said that during the October 3 protest in the New Delhi area, which sparked a "law and order situation", allegations of sexual harassment were made by three female journalists against police officers. "New Delhi District has received their complaints and the same are transferred to Crime Branch for fair and impartial enquiry."Following the allegations, several independent journalists held a protest outside Parliament Street police station, demanding FIRs against the officers.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: An Auckland father built his children a backyard roller coaster from scratch during lockdown; after testing it with 90kg of concrete, he is now selling the entire setup for NZ$4,500
articles.summary: During the COVID-19 lockdown, while most people were busy making dalgona coffee and baking banana bread, a father in Auckland was watching other people's
articles.body: During the COVID-19 lockdown, while most people were busy making dalgona coffee and baking banana bread, a father in Auckland was watching other people's backyard roller coasters on YouTube. Then he did what most of us never do after a video binge. He built one! That's right.Bjorn Burton built a roller coaster in his backyard. He started from scratch. He drew the plan, recruited his own dad for weekend labour, and turned a kids' playhouse into a working ride that snakes through the trees. Not a whisk in sight!All thanks to YouTubeIt was lockdown, so, like many others, Bjorn Burton also had a lot of time on his hands. He was on a binge-watch when he came across some backyard roller coaster videos. While most viewers would watch in surprise, admire them and go back to dinner, Burton decided to build one.He picked up a pencil. He designed the whole thing himself, then built it with weekend help from his own father. The playhouse was the straightforward part. The cart was another story. Constructing it turned out to be fiddly, slow work, and it took plenty of iterations and testing before he was happy with the result.Testing the rideBefore any child went near it, Burton wanted to know if it was safe. So he loaded the cart with bags of concrete totalling 90kg and sent it down the track. Once the ride ended, he repeated it again and again. The ride was carrying three times the weight it was meant to carry. The intended passenger limit was 30kg. But Burton wanted to make sure the roller coaster was safe. By the time a kid finally climbed in, he says, he was very confident about its safety. “I was very confident in its safety before we put one of the children down it,” he told the Evening Report.After the testing, he was content with the finished cart. It was a good one, but he had a small complaint. It reaches the end of the track a little faster than he would like! For a coaster designer, that is a fairly enviable problem.In the Burton household, time moved fast. The children, for whom the roller coaster was built, are much older now. The trees around the track have crept close enough to become a safety concern. So the coaster is going, and the playhouse is going with it.The Burtons are asking NZ$4,500 for the roller coaster, with pick-up from Cockle Bay, the outlet reported. Burton says the figure reflects the investment that went into building it. He is realistic about the market, though. “It’s a tough economic climate at the moment, but we’ve had a couple of offers that haven’t been too far off. I’m happy to price it to the market. We’ll see how it goes.”Now that it is finally time for the DIY roller coaster to go, Burton feels ‘a little bit jealous’. Why? Because, despite being the man who built it, Burton has never taken a ride. Adults are out of the question, he says, and the tight squeeze through the trees is only part of the reason. Weight would not be an issue, in his estimation. The real obstacle is the cart itself, which was made for children and which he doubts he could fit into. That doesn’t mean Burton would give up on the roller coaster. “Maybe one day, when I have grandchildren, I’ll build a bigger one!”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Not now daal-ing, says MAGA, as Montana governor comes to India to sell pulses
articles.summary: TOI correspondant from Washington: In Montana, ‘traffic’ is when you have to wait for three deer and a stray cow to cross the highway, so goes the joke
articles.body: TOI correspondant from Washington: In Montana, ‘traffic’ is when you have to wait for three deer and a stray cow to cross the highway, so goes the joke about a state where “just down the road” can mean a two-hour drive with no cellphone service. Yet for Montana Governor Greg Gianforte, one road this week stretches 8,000 miles, from the Big Sky State to India, home to 1.4 billion potential customers.Gianforte, a Republican, arrived in New Delhi on Monday at the head of a delegation of more than 30 Montanans representing agriculture, higher education, critical minerals, manufacturing, photonics, quantum technology and bioscience. The mission runs through October 9 and continues to Sri Lanka, and its major commercial pitch is deliciously simple: buy our daal, dahlings.Montana is America's largest producer of lentils and chickpeas and India is the world's largest consumer and importer of pulse crops. In 2025, however, India's purchases of Montana peas, lentils and chickpeas were for chicken feed, only about $14 million, which, along with commercial aircraft parts, made India Montana's 29th-largest trading partner.For a state of just over a million people – the population of an Indian mofussil town – India represents a huge opportunity. Montana's agricultural economy is substantial, but its producers need markets far beyond the state's borders, and indeed beyond the US and that is precisely where Gianforte's India trip collides with the conflict in Republican politics: the same MAGA constituency demanding that America buy American is also deeply suspicious when American governors go abroad to sell American products, particularly when the prospective customers are Indians.The backlash in this case has been instant and fierce. MAGA hardliners have questioned why Montana should deepen ties with India when, they argue, Indian students and faculty are "capturing" Montana universities.One viral discussion singled out Montana State University faculty with Indian roots, including Shivali Banerjee, an agricultural engineering professor with a PhD from IIT Bombay, and Sreekala and Dilpreet Bajwa, senior figures in the university's agriculture and engineering programs. Montana State's own records identify Sreekala Bajwa as vice president for agriculture and Dilpreet Bajwa as head of mechanical and industrial engineering.The irony is difficult to miss: Montana wants to sell agricultural products to India while some of its political activists are objecting to Indians teaching Montanans how to improve agriculture and engineering. "You need to be in America working for Americans, not jews or Indians. You are a traitor to the US,” one post aimed at Gianforte read.The controversy illustrates a growing bind for Republican governors, with Texas governor Greg Abbott facing a similar backlash in recent weeks. Their job is not to conduct immigration policy; it is to grow their states' economies. They want foreign investment, export markets, international students, researchers, and skilled workers, provided all of this produces jobs, tax revenue and prosperity at home. But the political language of the MAGA movement increasingly questions the efficacy of this model.Abbott, whose state has a bigger economy and larger Indian-origin population, has simultaneously cultivated Texas's enormous desi business community and taken a harder line on H-1B visas.In January, he ordered Texas state agencies and universities to freeze new H-1B petitions, arguing that jobs should go first to Texans. Yet he and other Texas Republicans are also aggressively courting Indian-American voters and business interests, creating an obvious tension between economic pragmatism and anti-immigration rhetoric from the MAGA base.Gianforte's dilemma is even more excruciating. Montana needs buyers; its farmers cannot sell lentils merely to Montanans, and its universities cannot become globally competitive by hiring only people born within state lines.And its emerging technology and scientific sectors cannot prosper by pretending talent stops at the adjoining Canadian border.There is a lesson for Gianforte from Montana’s own diplomatic history. Mike Mansfield, the state’s legendary senator and later ambassador to Japan, was a strong proponent in the 1960s of good ties with India.He was among the first lawmakers to appreciate India’s desire for strategic autonomy, and he understood that being from a small state should not inhibit big thinking. The foreign relations titan looked across the Pacific when much of America was looking inward, helping deepen US engagement with Asia, including India.Gianforte’s mission is more prosaic, selling Montana lentils, peas and chickpeas to India’s 1.4 billion people — but the principle is much the same: Big Sky country cannot afford small-world thinking.You use AI every day. articles.title: IDF pushes back on claim it targets journalists in Gaza, says 170 were part of terror groups, including Hamas
articles.summary: The IDF identified 170 alleged military operatives who reportedly worked as journalists while serving Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad in Gaza.
articles.body: The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) is pushing back against claims that it purposely targets journalists in Gaza, stating that individuals "presented as innocent journalists" were actually in Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) and other terrorist organizations. "They presented themselves as legitimate media professionals while serving terrorist organizations that regularly use propaganda and psychological warfare," the IDF stated on its website. "Journalists are expected to report the unbiased truth," the IDF continued. "Yet these individuals concealed a fundamental truth about themselves: their own roles within military wings of terrorist organizations." ISRAELI MEDICAL WORKERS WHO TREATED OCT 7 WOUNDED RELIVE DAY TERROR HIT HOME The IDF noted that targeting journalists is a violation of international law, but said that many articles, opinion pieces and reports have misled the public. As a result, the IDF launched an "in-depth investigation based on a wide range of intelligence sources, including open-source information, documents gathered in the field, interrogations of military operatives by Israeli intelligence bodies," to determine that claims the group violated international law do not tell the full story. The IDF listed 170 alleged military operatives who were reportedly working as journalists. For each person, the IDF lists the news outlet where the individual claimed to work, including some Western media organizations, while also listing the terror organization they have been linked to. For example, a person called Yaqoub Anan Mohammed Al-Barsh reportedly worked as a journalist for Gaza’s Namaa Radio but allegedly also held a position as a squad commander in the Military Propaganda Department of Hamas. MS RACHEL CALLS GAZA JOURNALIST ‘FRIEND’ IN RESURFACED CLIP AFTER HE ADMITS HIDING OCT 7 HOSTAGE FOOTAGE Another person, Maysara Ahmed Salah Salah, reportedly worked as a journalist for Quds News Network but was allegedly also a military operative for Hamas. Many of the 170 alleged military operatives identified by the IDF are seen in pictures wearing both press badges and holding weapons. Of the 170 individuals identified, 118 were operatives in Hamas, 49 in the Islamic Jihad’s military wing, one in the Lords of the Desert Terrorist Organization and two in the Popular Resistance Committees. All 170 have been killed. Hamas launched a war with an unprecedented Oct. 7, 2023, terror attack on Israel that resulted in the deaths of approximately 1,200 people, with Israeli civilians among those targeted. Hundreds of civilians were massacred at an outdoor music festival, others were slaughtered inside their homes, and Hamas took over 250 hostages in the worst attack on Jews since the Holocaust. ISRAEL'S NEW EXHIBIT EXPOSES YEARS OF HAMAS TERRORIST PLANNING BEFORE OCT 7 MASSACRE At least 17 of the individuals named by the IDF as terrorists masquerading as journalists were part of the group that infiltrated Israel during the Oct. 7 attacks, according to an IDF official. Other alleged terrorists posing as journalists have been honored by Reporters Without Borders, been named in complaints to the International Criminal Court and even used by the United Nations to condemn Israel, according to the IDF. This information emerged after the false narrative that the IDF deliberately targets journalists had already taken hold internationally," the IDF official told Fox News Digital. "Throughout the war, this narrative became one of the most frequently cited arguments against Israel," the continued. "It appeared in reports by international media outlets, human rights organizations, international institutions, and politicians, without distinguishing between journalists carrying out their professional duties and those who simultaneously operated as military operatives in terrorist organizations." articles.title: Loudoun school board urges students to ‘celebrate’ LGBTQ+ history in new proclamation
articles.summary: Loudoun County Public Schools defends its LGBTQ+ History Month proclamation as parents raise concerns over gender identity and locker room policies.
articles.body: Loudoun County Public Schools is defending its decision to recognize October as LGBTQ+ History Month, telling Fox News Digital that the school board proclamation imposes "no requirements" on students, even as the document encourages the school community to "honor and celebrate" LGBTQ+ history and contributions throughout the school year. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Loudoun County Public Schools said that the proclamation is a school board proclamation and that there are no requirements for students. The proclamation promises an "affirming" environment and rejects discrimination based on gender identity, sexual orientation and gender expression, raising questions about how the district’s language aligns with parents who object to schools promoting contested views about sex and gender. WASHINGTON FATHER SUES SCHOOL DISTRICT FOR DENYING RELIGIOUS OPT-OUT FOR 5TH GRADER FROM LGBTQ INSTRUCTION The proclamation reads in part, "Now, be it resolved that the Loudoun County School Board recognizes October 2026 as LGBTQ+ History Month in Loudoun County Public Schools, and encourages staff, students and the community to honor and celebrate the rich history and contributions of the LGBTQ+ community to the Commonwealth of Virginia, our beautifully diverse county, and our schools during LGBTQ+ History Month and throughout the school year." The proclamation also says that LCPS is "committed to fostering equity and belonging, ensuring students and staff members are welcomed into a safe, supportive, inclusive and affirming environment," and that it rejects "discrimination based on gender identity, sexual orientation or gender expression, and instead affirms kindness, acceptance and respect as the foundation of our learning community." PORTLAND PARENT BANNED FROM SCHOOL EVENTS AFTER OPPOSING GENDER IDENTITY ASSIGNMENT FILES LAWSUIT It also says that during the month of October as well as National Coming Out Day on Oct. 1, LCPS will "celebrate key figures and milestones, knowing that education is the most powerful tool to promote understanding and disrupt discrimination." LCPS has come under fire from parents due to various incidents reported of children at the school socially transitioning, as well as allegations of boys being in the girls' locker room and boys in the girls' bathrooms. DAD SUES AFTER SCHOOL ALLEGEDLY WON'T SAY IF BIOLOGICAL MALES CAN USE DAUGHTER'S BATHROOM One mother alleged that a biological girl who said she was transitioning to male came into the boys' bathroom and violated her son's privacy while he was at a urinal. articles.title: A tree crashed through a 1970 Atlanta homeowner's living room; a bad contractor left a $35,000 chimney problem before she recovered $57,000
articles.summary: A massive tree falling through an Atlanta home turned a familiar living space into the starting point of a months-long repair dispute for homeowner Judy
articles.body: A massive tree falling through an Atlanta home turned a familiar living space into the starting point of a months-long repair dispute for homeowner Judy Standard. The house, which she bought in 1970, suffered extensive damage to its chimney, roof, walls, deck and hardwood floors. What followed was another problem. The contractor Standard hired was not licensed for residential work and left important repairs unresolved. After an investigation by Atlanta News First, the situation took an unexpected turn, with Standard eventually receiving $57,000 through a contractor settlement and an additional insurance payment.What happened to the Atlanta homeowner after the tree crashed through her living roomJudy had lived near Cheshire Bridge Road in Atlanta since purchasing the house in 1970. According to Atlanta News First, the property had long been her home and was filled with natural light and her own paintings. That changed when a large tree crashed through the chimney and into the living room.The damage was extensive. State Farm estimated the repairs at $250,722, covering the roof, chimney, deck, walls and hardwood floors affected by water. The July 14 report from Atlanta News First said the insurance estimate was intended to cover the broad rebuilding work required after the accident.Standard needed someone to handle the repairs, and a contractor arrived at the property alongside her roofer. She said she did not know how the contractor had found out about the damage. She eventually hired him and signed over about $210,000 in insurance payments for the work.The contractor left behind a costly chimney problemThe contractor's crew completed much of the work, and Standard said several parts of the job were done well. The chimney, however, became a major concern. Atlanta News First reported that the contractor acknowledged he had not used the masonry company originally submitted to Standard's insurer because its quote was too expensive.A later inspection by another masonry company found the rebuilt chimney had been improperly constructed. The estimated cost to rebuild it correctly was $35,000, creating one of the most serious unresolved problems in the project. The July investigation also reported that $14,000 had been allocated for hardwood floor repairs, but Standard said no boards had actually been replaced.The problems were made more difficult by the contractor's credentials. Atlanta News First confirmed that he did not have a state-issued residential contractor's licence. He also had not obtained the required city permit for the work. The contractor acknowledged that the project was his first contracting job, according to the Atlanta News First report.What happened when Standard sought legal helpWith the repairs still unresolved, Standard turned to Atlanta Legal Aid. A pro bono senior attorney reviewed the case and sent the contractor a demand letter seeking $78,000 for incomplete or defective work, including the chimney.The contractor initially disagreed with the claims and considered the matter closed, according to Atlanta News First. However, after the investigation began asking questions, he agreed to meet Standard and her attorney. The meeting eventually led to a proposed $45,000 settlement. The July report said the contractor had agreed to that amount, although the payment had not yet been made at the time.How the homeowner ultimately recovered $57,000The outcome changed after Atlanta News First published its investigation. The broadcaster reported on August 18 that someone at State Farm saw the story and the insurer subsequently reevaluated Standard's claim.Two State Farm representatives then arrived at Standard's home and hand-delivered a $12,000 cheque. Atlanta News First said the additional payment came after the insurer reviewed the situation, although the report did not specify which particular repair accounted for the payment.The contractor's settlement also moved forward. Standard received a certified cheque for $45,000 from him, bringing the total amount she received through the two resolutions to $57,000.Lessons for homeowners from Standard's experienceThe case also highlighted the risks homeowners can face when trying to organise urgent repairs after major property damage. Atlanta News First reported that residential contractors working without the required state licence are not authorised to pull building permits. It also noted that policyholders are generally responsible for how insurance payments are distributed among contractors.State Farm offered several recommendations in its August report. The insurer advised homeowners to obtain multiple estimates, check a contractor's licence and insurance, verify references and insist on detailed written estimates. It also recommended staggering payments instead of paying everything in advance and keeping track of project costs.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Calling of a snap election was not a knee-jerk reaction from Pedro Sánchez but a carefully thought-out manoeuvre, Guy Hedgecoe reports from Madrid.
articles.body:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's decision to call a snap election for 29 November came on the back of a parliamentary defeat.

On Friday, the raft of measures he had presented to congress aimed at improving conditions for tenants and trying to address the problem of soaring rentals was narrowly rejected, as parties on the right voted against them.

That parliamentary result confirmed that Sánchez's left-wing coalition no longer commanded a majority.

But as has so often been the case throughout Sánchez's career, the calling of the election was not a knee-jerk reaction but a carefully thought-out manouevre.

His government has been struggling in recent months.

His Socialist Party has been mired in corruption, with cases implicating former senior figures in the party, Santos Cerdán and José Luis Ábalos, while the former Socialist Prime Minister, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, is facing accusations of having benefited financially from the government's bailout of an airline. Zapatero has denied wrongdoing.

In addition, Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, is due to go on trial over allegations of misuse of funds and influence peddling - accusations that Gómez and Sánchez vehemently deny.

Meanwhile, Sánchez's administration has struggled to manage the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa, where more than 70,000 migrants suddenly arrived in July. Most have returned over the border to Morocco, but the city has become a political and logistical headache for the prime minister.

Although Sánchez had insisted until recently that he would see out the legislature and not call elections until next summer, his government had looked increasingly unlikely to make it that far.

The wave of outrage which has exploded in recent days over housing has provided him with the ideal reason to call elections early - and a welcome issue away from Ceuta and the allegations of corruption.

Appealing to his own party's voters and those further to the left on Monday, he called for voters to "mobilise and ensure that parliament gives us a much bigger, progressive majority with which to defeat the elites, conquer social rights and keep transforming Spain".

On the upcoming campaign trail, Sánchez can point to the fact that his adversaries on the right - such as the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox - voted against his government's housing measures, which sought to prevent the eviction of tenants, improving the conditions of their contracts and preventing investors from buying residential property.

The PP and Vox tend to oppose any initiative presented by the Sánchez government, which they have long cast as illegitimate due to its scandals and reliance on Catalan and Basque nationalists.

However, as a matter of policy, parties on the right tend to oppose the kind of direct intervention in the housing market that Sánchez has been advocating, warning that it can be counterproductive.

Earlier this year, when Sánchez's international profile rose due to his outspoken criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and his clashes with US President Donald Trump, there was speculation that he might have used the political capital that gave him on the left and called an early election back then.

However, the housing issue, which is the biggest concern for Spaniards according to polls, appears more likely to mobilise support on the left.

Yet polls also show that the Socialists are trailing the PP. While the housing issue provides Sánchez with a potential fillip on the campaign trail, staying in power after these elections will be probably the biggest challenge of his career.

articles.title: Elderly woman used 7.7-pound amber nugget as doorstop for decades, unaware it was up to 70 million years old and worth €1 million; burglars stole gold but overlooked Romania’s rare ‘rumanite’ treasure
articles.summary: For decades, an elderly woman in Romania used what she believed was an ordinary reddish rock to keep her bedroom door open.
articles.body: For decades, an elderly woman in Romania used what she believed was an ordinary reddish rock to keep her bedroom door open. But after her death, the 7.7-pound (3.5-kilogram) object was identified as an exceptionally large piece of amber, estimated to be between 38.5 million and 70 million years old.According to a September 2024 report by EL PAIS, which cited Daniel Costache, director of the Buzau County Museum, the amber was found in the village of Colti in Buzau County and is now classified as a national treasure of Romania. The Buzau County Museum itself later listed the EL PAIS report among its international media appearances in its 2024 activity report.A doorstop hiding in plain sightThe woman reportedly found the unusual stone in a stream bed near her home in Colti, a village in southeastern Romania known for its amber deposits.She brought it home and used it as a simple doorstop for decades, apparently unaware that it was fossilized resin of extraordinary geological value.The story became even more remarkable because EL PAIS reported that burglars who broke into the woman's home stole gold jewellery but left the heavy amber nugget behind.The woman died in 1991. A relative who inherited the property subsequently became suspicious of the unusually heavy rock and arranged for it to be examined.Experts confirmed it was ancient amberRomanian authorities acquired the specimen and had it examined by specialists at the History Museum in Krakow, Poland.According to EL PAIS, the Krakow specialists confirmed that the object was genuine amber and estimated its age at between 38.5 million and 70 million years.The specimen weighs approximately 3.5 kilograms, making it one of the largest intact amber pieces known. It is now held by the Buzau County Museum and has been on display there since 2022.Estimated value of around €1 millionThe amber has frequently been reported as being worth around €1 million, or roughly $1.1 million.However, the figure should be treated as an estimate rather than a confirmed sale price. EL PAIS quoted museum director Daniel Costache as saying the discovery has major scientific and museum significance, underscoring that its importance extends well beyond its monetary value.The Buzau County Museum has also been careful about claims describing the specimen as the world's largest amber or rumanite nugget, with unofficial record titles differing between reports.Why the Romanian amber is unusualThe amber comes from the Buzau region, where deposits of reddish and dark-coloured fossilized resin are found around Colti.Locally known as chihlimbar, the material is also referred to as rumanite and is distinguished by its deep red, brown and almost black shades.Amber forms when tree resin becomes buried and undergoes chemical and geological changes over millions of years. Unlike sap, which transports water and nutrients through a tree, resin is produced as a protective substance, helping trees seal wounds and defend against insects and disease.A window into prehistoric environmentsLarge pieces of amber can be scientifically valuable because resin may trap insects, plant material and air bubbles before becoming buried.Such inclusions can preserve biological material in three dimensions and provide researchers with clues about prehistoric ecosystems and environmental conditions.The Romanian specimen's size makes it particularly notable, as most pieces of raw amber found in nature are much smaller.You use AI every day. articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir high court quashed the preventive detention of a man booked under the Public Safety Act (PSA) on charges of showing a
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir high court quashed the preventive detention of a man booked under the Public Safety Act (PSA) on charges of showing a disposition towards anti-national activities, terming the allegations against him “prima facie vague”.The detention of Mashooq Ahmad Shah of Shahlatoo was in violation of constitutional guarantees envisaged under Article 22(5) of the Constitution, Justice Rajnesh Oswal said in his order Saturday, directing his immediate release if he was not wanted in any other case.The Shopian district magistrate on Dec 23, 2025, ordered the detention of Shah based on a police dossier that cited intelligence reports and said that he had “shown a tendency towards anti-national activities in his locality and other parts of the district ... and hatred against the state and govt in order to radicalise and instigate the youth towards anti-national activities”.The dossier further mentioned that Shah “remains a perpetual concern for the security agencies” and “could potentially be used as a conduit by terrorist outfits to build underground networks”. His conduct indicated “he has no respect for judicial proceedings and the law of the land”, it added.Shah was lodged in Jammu’s Kot Bhalwal jail. He moved the HC, arguing that the grounds of detention were false, incorrect, vague and non-existent. The allegations “are illusory and without any material basis”, he said.Justice Oswal concurred with the petitioner that the charges against him were vague and “bereft of necessary particulars”. The court said the state failed to identify the persons and associations with extremist leanings with which it alleged Shah maintained contact, nor did it specify who the youths were with whom the petitioner attempted to establish contact and when.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: About 5 billion lbs of carpet are removed from US buildings each year; a cement kiln test found it worked as fuel, but transport costs were too high
articles.summary: Approximately 5 billion lbs of carpet will be removed from buildings in the US each year for the foreseeable future, according to a report by Georgia Tech
articles.body: Approximately 5 billion lbs of carpet will be removed from buildings in the US each year for the foreseeable future, according to a report by Georgia Tech Research Corporation. The face of that carpet contains plastic that can be reused, but it is held in place by a latex cross-linked polymer heavily loaded with calcium carbonate. The report states that this backing has almost no value as a recycled material. Researchers then burnt carpet as fuel at Lehigh Cement's kiln in Evansville, Pennsylvania. Carpet proved technically suitable, yet the report concludes that the economic barriers were too high.Why carpet is being studied as an alternative fuel in cement kilnsCarpet tile is typically made for the commercial market and has a heavier backing, often PVC. According to the final report, Carpet As An Alternative Fuel in Cement Kilns, PVC tiles are, at the time of the report, handled through a recycling system run by Interface or Tandus, so they were excluded from the study. Broadloom, in contrast, "is not recycled in significant volumes compared to its sales" and is the subject of the report. Broadloom comes with two backing types, an SB latex and a polyurethane foam back, and with two face constructions: level loop and tufted.For latex-backed carpet, the report lists four main components: the face fibre, the primary backing layer, the filled latex glue layer and the secondary backing layer. It states that the face fibre is typically nylon 6, nylon 66 or polypropylene, with smaller amounts of PET and wool. The primary and secondary backings are polypropylene. The latex styrene butadiene glue is "typically filled with calcium carbonate, fly ash, or ground glass." The report notes that the two backing types affect the products of combustion and the melting points: the polyurethane backing tends to melt if it gets too hot, while the latex does not.How calcium carbonate affects carpet as an alternative fuelThe executive summary describes how the carpet is held together. The face is woven through a backing fabric and held in place by a "glue" that is, in most cases, a latex cross-linked polymer heavily loaded with chalk (calcium carbonate). The report states directly that "this backing has almost no value as a recycled material." It also describes carpet as a bulky material that is difficult to handle and ship and must be kept dry.Table 1 of the report, from the SB Latex Carpet Life Cycle Inventory by Dr Michael Overcash, gives a representative composition for a final product of 1.92 kg per square yard. The entries are calcium carbonate at 0.48 kg, nylon 6 fibre at 0.81 kg, polypropylene at 0.18 kg, aluminium hydroxide at 0.24 kg and SB latex at 0.21 kg. Stain blocker is listed at 1.89E-04 kg and other additives at 1.29E-03 kg. The report also says the filler content influences how abrasive the material is during size reduction, and that calcium carbonate causes aggressive wear on cutting surfaces.How carpet performed as an alternative fuel in a cement kiln trialThe project's research question was whether carpet could be used as a fuel in a cement kiln. The trial took place at Lehigh Cement's long dry kiln at Evansville, Pennsylvania. The report records that carpet was burnt at rates approximating 10–15% of the fuel load, at about 2–2.5 tons per hour, and that this did not negatively impact the kiln's emissions. According to Table 9, NOx and SO2 emissions were below the allowed limits for both coal and carpet co-firing, although SO2 appeared higher for carpet. The report concludes that "carpet was technically a suitable fuel."The existing feed system, designed for wood chips, would jam unless closely supervised, and only 200 tons of the targeted 1000 tons were fed. On economics, the report states that carpet was worth approximately 1.2 c/lb as a fuel, based on coal at about $1.60 per mmbtu and 7500 btu/lb. Actual freight was $550 per load over 100 miles, which the report says "immediately wipes out the value of the carpet." It concludes that "the economic barriers to the adoption of carpet at this kiln are too high."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: I tried the viral Skylight Calendar to organize my family’s chaos — here’s what won me over
articles.summary: From color-coded scheduling to screen-free morning routines, here’s an honest look at how Skylight’s Calendar, Frame and Buddy actually work for busy families.
articles.body: Over the past few years, Skylight has carved out a reputation for helping people bring a little more order and ease into their daily life. The brand’s first product, the Skylight Frame, launched in 2015 to help people get photos out of people’s phones and on display in their homes. Since then, the brand launched a digital calendar and a routine-building alarm clock for kids, both of which aim to help households run more smoothly. Moms in particular rave about how their products alleviate the mental load of having to remember to do things like send grandparents photos, schedule appointments and sign kids up for extracurricular activities. But with products costing upwards of $160, is this brand worth the hype (and price tag)? Over the years, I have tested everything Skylight has to offer, as have a few other NBC Selected editors (and some former editors). Keep reading to get all the details on what we really think. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. Our honest review of Skylight This is the updated version of the product that put Skylight on the map (though the original is also still available). The upgraded version has an HD anti-glare touchscreen that allows you to pinch, crop and zoom, swappable magnetic frames and 16GB of storage, which gives you room for up to 16,000 photos. “It’s simple to set up — I’m confident almost anyone could do it with little issue,” says former NBC Selected reporter Harry Rabinowitz, who tested the frame extensively. After receiving the device, you just plug it in, connect to WiFi and create a unique Skylight email address. From there, friends and family can send photos instantly by email or through the free Skylight app, and they’ll appear on the frame within seconds. I purchased this frame for my parents last Christmas because my mom was constantly asking me to send her pics of my two kids, and I found this to be a much easier way of sharing what was going on in their lives. I love that Skylight lets you set up the frame and preload it with photos before gifting it, so it’s ready to go the moment your recipient plugs it in. The frame also offers a degree of personalization and versatility. The magnetic frames let you swap styles in seconds (simply clip it on the top edges around the screen); you can choose from real hardwood, aluminum or classic colored finishes to match any room’s decor. As a mom of two, I can tell you that there’s a particular kind of chaos that comes with juggling school pickups, sports practices, work meetings, doctor appointments and more for four different people. Which is why, when a fellow working mom told me that the Skylight Calendar had alleviated her mental load, I was intrigued. The WiFi-enabled calendar is intended to serve as a family’s organizational hub. One of the features that won me over quickly was the color-coding system. Every family member gets assigned their own color, so at a glance you can tell whose dentist appointment is Tuesday and whose dance practice runs late on Thursday, without squinting at tiny text or scrolling through a shared app. You can also color-code by activity type instead of person, which is handy if you’d rather see all your work commitments in one color and all the kids’ school events in another. Either way, the effect is the same: a wall calendar that actually reads clearly from across the room, instead of one big wall of black text. Another function I love? You don’t have to manually enter everything. You can take photos of events or flyers and email them (or use the app to upload them) straight to your calendar to be automatically input. The calendar also doubles as a running grocery list and chore chart, which cuts down on two more apps I used to juggle. Anyone in the family can add items to the shared grocery list right from the screen (or a companion app), so it updates in real time instead of relying on someone remembering to text the last person heading to the store. The chore chart works similarly: you can assign tasks to specific kids, set them to repeat daily or weekly, and let your kids check things off themselves, which can cut down on the, “did you do your chores?” back-and-forth happening in so many households. Worth noting: the core calendar, chore chart and lists all work right out of the box with no subscription needed. If you want extras like meal planning, the photo/video screensaver or chore rewards, though, you’ll need to pay for Skylight Plus, which runs for about $79 a year. If your household has ample real estate to see everyone’s schedule at once, there’s also the Skylight Calendar Max, a 27-inch version built exclusively for wall mounting. It has all the same core features as the standard Calendar, including the color-coding, chore charts, grocery lists and photo import, just on a much bigger display, which makes it a better fit for larger families or anyone who wants their calendar visible from across the room rather than up close. Buddy is Skylight’s latest release and its goal is getting kids through mornings and bedtimes without a parent repeating the same instructions five times. In other words, it’s my favorite new device. The screen allows your kid to see their routine laid out step by step — get dressed, brush teeth, get in bed — and tap a button after each one, earning stars and a small on-screen celebration for finishing. It’s a deliberately limited device: no apps, no browser, no way to drift into unrelated screen time once the routine is done, which is part of what makes it easy to hand to a young kid without hesitation. Parents set everything up and manage it remotely through the same app used for the Skylight Calendar. My 5-year-old daughter has been using Buddy for three months now, and I’ve been amazed by how much it helps her stick to a routine and feel confident about going about her day. She doesn’t need me hovering or repeating myself, she just checks the screen and knows what’s next, which has made our mornings noticeably calmer. Beyond the routines, Buddy also lets kids earn rewards for completing tasks consistently, which parents can customize to fit whatever motivates their own child. For example, every time my daughter makes her bed and checks off the task on her Buddy, she gets a digital star. Once she has 20 stars, I’ve set it up so the Buddy lets her know she’s completed a goal and I take her out for ice cream. For families juggling multiple kids or hectic schedules, it’s a small addition that’s made a surprisingly big difference. What can improve After spending time testing Skylight’s lineup, a few things stood out as room for growth: Subscription gating: Across all three products, some genuinely useful features (video playback and albums on the Frame, rewards and nudges on Buddy, some list features on the Calendar) sit behind a paid plan rather than being included with the hardware purchase.Price of entry: Between the Calendar, a Frame for the grandparents and a Buddy for each kid, outfitting a whole household in Skylight products adds up quickly compared to using a shared family calendar app or a single all-purpose smart display. How I tested Skylight To find out how Skylight’s devices hold up beyond first impressions, I made them part of my everyday routine and pushed them the way a busy household would. Real-life scenarios: I used them in everyday situations rather than staged demos, stress testing how they performed when it counted.Every available feature: I tried each feature on offer, not just the headline ones, to see which ones were actually useful.Daily interaction: I used them every day to make sure they stayed practical once the novelty wore off. Who is Skylight for? Skylight is for anyone who wants to simplify basic tasks and help their lives run a bit more smoothly. Their products are particularly good for families who may be tight on time or who need help staying organized. Each product in the brand’s bestselling lineup has a unique purpose: The calendar is great for anyone juggling multiple calendars, while the Frame is helpful for those who take a lot of photos or want to share them with loved ones. Finally, the Buddy is perfect for a kid who is learning to be more independent and needs help sticking to routines. If you are on a budget and looking for most budget-friendly alternatives, Amazon has a number of options — but keep in mind you won’t get all the same features with the lower-priced alternatives. For example, the Max Angel Digital Frame ($69.99) displays photos similar to Skylight’s frame but you can’t zoom in. And the Dragon Touch Digital Calendar ($79.99) is much smaller than the Skylight Calendar 2 and is best for families looking for simple calendar keeping without all the other features. Why trust NBC Selected? I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers wellness, beauty, home and lifestyle. I have written about honey skin care, the Jellycat craze and more. I have been using a Skylight calendar in my home for over a year and recently got my 5-year-old daughter the Buddy. Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

articles.title: Former 'American Idol' contestant sentenced to life without parole for wife's murder
articles.summary: Caleb Flynn was found guilty of murdering his wife, Ashley Flynn.
articles.body:
An Ohio man who was found guilty of murdering his wife and staging the crime scene to make it seem as if an intruder had broken into their home and fatally shot the mother of two was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Caleb Flynn, 40, a former pastor who once appeared as a contestant on "American Idol" in 2013, was found guilty of aggravated murder and multiple counts of murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence in connection with the death of his wife, 37-year-old Ashley Flynn.

Judge Jeannine Pratt called the former pastor's actions "abhorrent" and "quite honestly impossible to fathom" while handing down the life sentence on Monday.

Caleb Flynn called 911 early on Feb. 16 to report that his wife had been shot by an intruder at their home in Tipp City, north of Dayton. He was arrested three days later. Prosecutors alleged that Caleb Flynn "executed" his wife by shooting her twice in the back of the head in bed so that he could be with his mistress and manipulated the crime scene to make it seem as if an intruder had broken in through the garage.

Pratt said that after considering the evidence in the case, there is "one clear and obvious conclusion" -- that Caleb Flynn poses the "highest risk" of harm to the public -- and admonished the "layers of deceit, manipulation and cruelty" that he has shown.

"You could have walked away. You could have separated from her and left her here on this earth to be able to be with the people that need her, who loved her, who looked forward to having her in their lives. But instead, through your greed, your selfishness, your lust, and your cruelty, you chose to take Ashley's life, and in doing so, you did far more than take the life of your wife," Pratt said. "On that fateful day in February, the person who should have been protecting their children shattered their lives."

Caleb Flynn addressed the court prior to learning his sentence, crying while reading from prepared remarks that he shakily clutched while in handcuffs and an orange jumpsuit.

He repeatedly denied killing his wife, saying, "I have unfortunately lied about a lot of things over the last couple of years. But as I stand here before God, who is my ultimate judge, I am not lying when I say I did not kill my wife."

"I will continue to fight for my innocence as long as the Lord allows me to, since I did not kill my wife," he said.

He apologized to his wife's family and asked for their forgiveness.

"I made vows to Ashley on our wedding day -- I failed those vows, and through my decisions, I have caused you guys an incredible amount of pain," he said. "Through those decisions, I'm sure you have felt betrayal, confusion, anger and so much more."

"I take complete accountability for my words and my decisions," he said. "I am so sorry, I am so sorry, and pray that you can one day forgive me."

Caleb Flynn also addressed members of his family, including his young daughters.

"I don't know if they'll ever be able to hear this, but I want them to hear it regardless -- I love you two," he said, calling them his "greatest joy in his life."

He apologized for not being able to see them grow up and said through tears that he misses them "more than you'll ever know."

The judge said she received over a dozen victim impact statements, and several members of Ashley Flynn's family addressed the court prior to the sentence being handed down, speaking to the impact the murder of their mother has had on his daughters, Alyssa and Ava, and asking for the maximum possible sentence.

In a searing letter read on her behalf, Alyssa said, "You have already caused so much pain to your family and the world. The least you can do is tell everyone you did it and receive your outcome."

"Did you really even think about how much pain you would bring your own two daughters?" the statement continued. "By the way, Ashley Flynn was the best thing that ever happened to you. You had the best life ever, and you decided to throw it away for a girl who was half your age."

In closing, she said her family has "never been stronger" and she doesn't plan to visit him in prison.

He faced up to life in prison without parole.

Prosecutors asked for the maximum possible sentence, arguing in a sentencing memorandum filed ahead of the hearing that he is a "dangerous individual with no regard for human life and has refused to accept accountability or show any remorse."

" It is important to note that Defendant could have lawfully left his marriage. Instead, he chose murder. He planned Ashley's murder for months. This was a planned and calculated execution," Prosecuting Attorney Paul Watkins stated.

In his memo, Watkins said Caleb Flynn's "effort to escape responsibility did not end with the staged scene or the false intruder narrative," but that his two daughters described him instructing them on what to say in their forensic interviews and that their statements "could be the difference between life and death for him."

"Thus, after taking their mother from them, Defendant attempted to use his grieving daughters to reinforce the story he had created to protect himself," Watkins stated.

The defense, meanwhile, said in its memorandum that Flynn continues to maintain his innocence and has no prior criminal history while asking for a sentence that "preserves the possibility of parole and a return to society following his rehabilitation."

The jury deliberated for nearly 2 1/2 hours before reaching a verdict on Sept. 29, finding him guilty of all charges.

During closing arguments, Miami County Assistant Prosecutor Matthew Joseph pointed to evidence including the physical scene and a side garage door he said was made to look as if an intruder had damaged it, Caleb Flynn's 911 call, text messages between the defendant and his mistress discussing the end of his marriage and digital records from the night of the shooting, which he argued "leads straight to the defendant."

"The evidence showed that being the victim would allow the defendant to keep his lucrative job working for Ashley's family business, he would benefit from Ashley's life insurance, and he could keep his position as a working worship leader with zero impact to his reputation within the church," Joseph said during closing arguments on Sept. 29 in the Miami County courtroom. "The evidence does not tell the story of an intruder."

Defense attorney Patrick Mulligan argued during his closing that the state's evidence is circumstantial, and that the only thing prosecutors proved was that Caleb Flynn was having an affair.

"Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn't solve the case," Mulligan told jurors.

Caleb Flynn did not testify during the trial and the defense called no witnesses.

He denied killing his spouse in an interview with police days after the deadly shooting, according to video shown during the more than weeklong trial.

His former mistress testified for the state during the trial, reading from some of the more than 100,000 messages they exchanged over her two days of testimony.

"If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat," Caleb Flynn said in one message from May 2025, Botner testified .

Following the guilty verdict, Mulligan told reporters that he expected there to be a notice of appeal filed.

When asked what appellate issues they have, he said, "There's a lack of evidence on prior calculation and design."

Watkins thanked the jury "for their dedication to justice in this case."

In a statement read by Watkins, Ashley Flynn's family said they "refuse to let the evil that ended Ashley's life have the final word in her story."

"Ashley loved Jesus with her whole heart. Her faith wasn't simply something she simply spoke about. It was how she lived," the statement said. "She loved people well, found joy beyond her circumstances, prayed boldly for her family, and wanted her life to point people to Jesus."

"Most of all, she loved being a mom," the statement continued. "She prayed over her girls, taught them to love God, and showed them what it looked like to live with faith, kindness, joy, and grace."

articles.title: GP appointment time 'making it harder to do cancer checks'
articles.summary: Dr Amara Naseem says appointment times are not long enough to get the information she needs.
articles.body:
Pressure to provide more GP appointments is making it harder to include checks for gynaecological cancers within the 10-minute slots, doctors have said.

Dr Amara Naseem says her clinics always overrun as it takes about 20 minutes to sensitively take a detailed history and carry out internal examinations.

A reduced number of practices in her area means she has taken on more patients and fears there is a risk that women will not raise gynaecological symptoms or attend screenings if appointments are rushed, painful or not handled well.

The Welsh government said it was increasing investment in primary care and recruiting up to 100 extra GPs.

Research by cancer charity Tenovus, in support of Claire's Campaign , found about half of the 100 GPs surveyed across Wales felt limited consultation time was a major concern.

A third also had concerns about "over-referring" people for further testing to rule out cancers, given hospitals are already overstretched.

Currently, 95% of patients put on the suspected cancer pathway are later told they do not have cancer.

But doctors said teasing out the cancer cases at an early stage could be challenging when symptoms such as bloating are hard to distinguish from benign conditions including irritable bowel syndrome.

Naseem said the pressure from the Welsh government was to "offer more appointments to the patient, rather than about the quality of the treatment".

Lowri Griffiths of Tenovus said incidence and mortality rates for gynaecological cancers in Wales were higher than the UK average - something she added the Welsh government needed "to get to grips with".

Pledges to increase GP numbers were promising, she said, "but unless we address both the primary care setting and the hospital setting, the system won't work".

Naseem said many women's health issues may require an internal examination, which requires time to be done "in an empathetic and sensitive way".

She added: "I'm working in a very diverse community, also in a deprived community, where uptake of screening is already low."

She said in communities where myths existed around screening, time is also required to explain what is involved and allay fears and potentially work with interpreters.

Dr Kathrin Thomas, a former GP and public health specialist, got involved in Claire's Campaign when her friend Claire O'Shea was given a late diagnosis for a gynaecological cancer.

Claire, from Cardiff, died last year, aged 42.

Thomas said GP numbers in Wales had "almost flat-lined" while the workload had increased, especially in more disadvantaged areas where there were "fewer doctors, fewer nurses and the healthcare needs are much greater".

She is also involved with Deep End Cymru - a network of GP practices in the most deprived areas.

"We've got a big difference in the cancer experience in more deprived communities - cervical cancer in particular," she said.

"There's a wide inequity between women in more affluent areas and women in poorer areas."

Of the 1,200 women diagnosed, about 470 patients die from a gynaecological cancer, either of the womb (uterine), ovary, cervix, vulva or vagina, in Wales each year.

Screening is only available for cervical cancer and it does not detect other cancers.

"Cancer outcomes are improving dramatically over the decades, but we're struggling in Wales to get the outcomes that other richer countries are getting," said Thomas.

The waiting times for gynaecological cancer treatment in Wales have improved significantly over the past year, from 34% of patients being treated within 62 days, to 51.3%.

However, the most recent Wales average for all cancers was 60.1% against a target of 75%.

Thomas said continuity of care came up repeatedly among the Tenovus survey of GPs.

"You have a 20% less chance of dying if you have the same team that looks after you," she said.

Maria Bailey feels being able to see the same GP was a factor in her own cervical cancer diagnosis.

"I feel really lucky that she took me seriously from the off. She knows me - she knew I was alarmed and [the symptoms] weren't normal for me. She took it very seriously," she said.

The 55-year-old from Pencoed, Bridgend county, experienced increased fatigue and light vaginal bleeding but put it down to working extra hours and the menopause.

But in February she spoke to her GP after the bleeding intensified.

"It was heavy bleeding and quite large clots, which I've never had before - they looked like baby seals and that was really alarming."

An internal examination followed by a raft of further tests uncovered a 4cm (1.5in) tumour and grade 2 cancer around her cervix.

"I was in shock, but as soon as they said it wasn't life-threatening, that was it. It was just one gear - and that was go."

Maria underwent chemotherapy, radiotherapy and brachytherapy across centres in Swansea and Cardiff and has since been raising money to provide essential provisions for others going through treatment for cervical cancer.

"I'm quite an organised person and don't like walking into anything blind," she said.

But an online search for advice about the things needed when starting treatment yielded very little.

She has now donated several "Bailey's bags" to two cancer centres containing items such as a water bottle, strong-flavoured sweets to overcome the metallic taste treatment can leave, a foldable fan, neck cushion, battery pack for USB devices and a medication box.

The Welsh government said: "We're committed to strengthening primary care as the foundation of the NHS in Wales.

"We've urged health boards to shift more resources towards primary and community care, with a further primary care summit planned to track their progress.

"We're updating our women's health plan to make sure women's voices are heard, and transforming how the NHS prevents, diagnoses and treats cancer through our 10-year national cancer strategy, with a focus on earlier diagnosis."

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BJP on Monday did not renominate two Union ministers, Hardeep Singh Puri and B L Verma, as its Rajya Sabha picks from Uttar Pradesh, rekindling
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP on Monday did not renominate two Union ministers, Hardeep Singh Puri and B L Verma, as its Rajya Sabha picks from Uttar Pradesh, rekindling speculation that PM Narendra Modi is looking to reshuffle his council of ministers as vacancies rise.Two other ministers, Ravneet Singh Bittu and George Kurien, were similarly left out of Rajya Sabha nominations in June, leading to their resignation. While these two were state ministers, a position held by Verma as well, Puri is a Cabinet minister holding the crucial portfolio of petroleum and natural gas.His likely exit from the Cabinet after the then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan quit in July following CJP's stir over paper leaks further makes the case of a reshuffle as both are demanding portfolios. Consumer affairs, food and public distribution minister Pralhad Joshi is currently handling the education ministry as an additional charge.A minister since Sep 2017, former diplomat Puri is the lone Sikh face in the council of ministers and had unsuccessfully contested the Lok Sabha election from Amritsar in 2019.Whether BJP deploys Puri for Punjab polls remains to be seenSome Union ministers like Pankaj Chaudhary and Harsh Malhotra, now heading BJP’s state units in UP and Delhi respectively, have been given organisation responsibilities in an indication that their continuation in govt is unlikely to continue beyond the expected reshuffle.Puri’s term as Rajya Sabha MP from UP ends in Nov, and rules allow a minister to hold his office for six months without being an MP. Not having much of a political constituency of his own, it remains to be seen if he, like Bittu, will be deployed in the Punjab assembly polls, scheduled to be held along with four other states, including UP, early next year.While the impending Punjab election was cited by some experts as a case for his continuation due to his Sikh background, BJP brass in the end chose to not repeat any of its RS candidates, a practice it had followed in the last round of elections as well.Since taking over as PM in 2014, Modi has gone for an overhaul of his council of ministers before the mid-term in both his earlier stints, giving rise to the prospect of a major rejig as his govt is now well into its third year in its third stint.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
