articles.title: China’s Fuman Oilfield, largest desert oilfield, extracts 26.86 million tons of oil and gas from below 6,000 metres; engineers recover 500-million-year-old rock core from record 8,080-metre depth in Xinjiang
articles.summary: China’s largest desert oilfield has extracted more than 26 million tons of oil and gas from ultra-deep formations beneath the Taklimakan Desert, marking a
articles.body: China’s largest desert oilfield has extracted more than 26 million tons of oil and gas from ultra-deep formations beneath the Taklimakan Desert, marking a major milestone in the country’s push to tap increasingly difficult underground reserves.The Fuman Oilfield, located on the northern edge of the Taklimakan Desert in northwest China’s Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, has produced a combined 26.86 million tons of oil and gas equivalent, according to China National Petroleum Corp. (CNPC), which operates the field.The milestone comes as engineers explore formations buried thousands of metres beneath the surface, with a recent drilling operation retrieving rock cores from a depth of 8,080 metres.Rock core recovered from 8,080 metres undergroundAt the Zhentan-1 well on the edge of the Taklimakan Desert, engineers recently brought rock cores to the surface from 8,080 metres below ground.According to a report by China Central Television (CCTV) News, the rocks have been buried for approximately 500 million years. The operation marks the first time China has retrieved a core sample from a depth exceeding 8,000 metres in the northwestern Tarim Basin.The samples could provide scientists and petroleum engineers with important information about the geological formations beneath the desert.“With these precious rock cores, we can analyze and evaluate the hydrocarbon generation potential below 8,000 meters, including the thickness of the oil and gas layers and their maturity levels,” Xu Yanan, director of the Tarim Oilfield project at CNPC, was quoted as saying by CCTV News.More than 20 million tons of crude oil extractedThe Fuman Oilfield's ultra-deep production has already reached substantial levels.According to Lu Zhongyuan, an engineer with CNPC's Tarim Oilfield, the operation has extracted 20.36 million tons of crude oil and 8.15 billion cubic metres of natural gas from ultra-deep formations beneath the Taklimakan Desert.Together, that production represents an oil and gas equivalent of more than 26.86 million tons, Lu said, according to CCTV News.The figures underline the scale of China's efforts to develop hydrocarbon resources buried at depths that present major technical challenges for drilling and extraction.485 ultra-deep wells drilledIn recent years, the Tarim Oilfield has accelerated ultra-deep oil and gas exploration and production beneath the Taklimakan Desert.A total of 485 ultra-deep wells have been drilled at the Fuman Oilfield, according to media reports. Of those, 133 wells have each produced more than 100,000 tons of oil and gas, while 464 wells have each produced more than 10,000 tons.The development has helped establish the Tarim Oilfield as China's largest desert oilfield and a major ultra-deep hydrocarbon production base.Tarim Basin holds vast ultra-deep reservesThe Taklimakan Desert sits in the heart of the Tarim Basin, a vast inland basin in southern Xinjiang that contains significant oil and gas resources.The basin's ultra-deep formations are considered an important potential source for increasing China's domestic hydrocarbon reserves and production.According to the information cited by Chinese state media, China has already proven more than 5 billion tons of oil and gas reserves in the Tarim Basin, with more than half located in ultra-deep formations at depths exceeding 6,000 metres.The latest rock-core recovery from 8,080 metres could help researchers better understand these formations and assess whether additional hydrocarbon resources exist even deeper beneath the desert.A new frontier for ultra-deep energy explorationThe scale and depth of the Fuman Oilfield development highlight the increasingly challenging environments being targeted by China's energy industry.Recovering geological samples from more than eight kilometres below the surface allows researchers to directly examine rocks that have remained buried for hundreds of millions of years.For CNPC, the data gathered from these cores could help determine the thickness, maturity and hydrocarbon-generation potential of deep geological formations, potentially guiding future exploration across the Tarim Basin.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mettur storage down, delta has barely 10 days of irrigation water
articles.summary: Mettur dam storage falls to 34 tmcft, leaving Cauvery delta with about 10 days of irrigation water; releases for samba crops may stop after Oct 14.
articles.body: Chennai: Cauvery delta districts may have water for irrigating paddy crops of the samba season for another 10 days at best, due to a sharp fall in the storage of Mettur dam, say govt officials. The situation has triggered another round of concern among farmers.According to water resources department officials, Mettur dam had 34.046tmcft (thousand million cubic feet) of water as of Monday evening, with the level at 71.5ft. Officials said water could be released for irrigation for the delta region only until the storage drops to 20tmcft.“We are releasing 15,000 cusecs for irrigation and drinking water needs. If the rate of depletion continues and there is no rain in the catchment area of Cauvery, we will not be able to release water for samba cultivation from Oct 14,” the official said.Once the storage falls to 20tmcft, the outflow will be reduced to 1,200-1,500 cusecs to meet drinking water needs. The supply will be maintained for Veeranam, while the supply for Grand Anaicut would dry up, officials said. This would deprive farmers in delta districts who have raised paddy of water.“Poor rainfall and the shortfall in releasing the stipulated share of Cauvery water by Karnataka have contributed to the decline in storage,” said a senior WRD official. Despite Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) directing Karnataka to release the stipulated quantity of water on a pro rata basis, it did not adhere to the direction nor comply with the Supreme Court order, the officer said.In the 58th meeting held on Sept 24, CWMA instructed Karnataka to release 4,000 cusecs of water to Tamil Nadu for 15 days. But what Tamil Nadu was receiving at Biligundulu was less than 2,000 cusecs for the past several days and further dropped to 1,424 cusecs at 4pm on Monday, said officials.“Since the beginning of the water year in June, up to Oct 1, Karnataka should have released 123.7tmcft of water to Tamil Nadu. But it has released only 44.4tmcft, leaving a deficit of 79.3tmcft,” said the official.The situation has renewed concerns among farmers, who have urged Tamil Nadu govt to get Karnataka to release the water.“The flow of Cauvery water in the river is not sufficient. Water has not reached the A channels completely on either side of the riverbanks in the delta region. Several B, C and D channels, as well as smaller branch channels, are yet to receive water, leaving farmers uncertain about raising their crops. If this is the situation now, it will become even more critical for farmers if we do not receive water from Mettur after October 14,” said Swamimalai S Vimalnathan, secretary of the TN Cauvery Farmers’ Protection Association.He said officials appeared to be under the impression that the entire delta had received water once it reached the tail-end areas. “That is far from the ground reality,” he said.“Direct sowing is also not suitable in all areas. articles.title: ‘Smash the patriarchy’: Activists graffiti Cornell hall over gang rape case
articles.summary: Student groups call for the abolition of Greek life and more punitive action in the wake of fraternity assault allegations.
articles.body:
Protesters in the United States have shattered a glass door at Cornell University’s main administrative headquarters and spray-painted messages on the building’s walls as backlash continues following allegations about a 2024 gang rape at a local fraternity.

In the early hours of Monday, the glass panes on an entrance door for the building, Day Hall, were smashed, leaving shards strewn across the floor.

Activists, outraged at the school’s handling of the case, also graffitied nearby walls with slogans like “At Cornell rapists are protected protesters are expelled” and “Smash the patriarchy”.

The predawn incident came ahead of a rally demanding “justice for survivors” by student groups on Monday.

Cornell spokesperson Kyle Kimball said Monday that the university was investigating the vandalism.

“We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community,” Kimball said. “Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer.”

Cornell, a prominent Ivy League university in the state of New York, has been at the centre of a national firestorm over sexual violence on US campuses, after an anonymous student, Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit last month alleging a gang rape at the fraternity Chi Phi.

Her complaint accuses seven former students of perpetrating “heinous criminal sexual acts” against her during a fraternity party on the night of October 19, 2024, after she says she was pressured to drink and take the drug ketamine.

The fraternity, Cornell University and others are named as co-defendants in the suit. Lawyers for two of the former students have rejected claims that they participated in sexual assault.

The case has elicited outcry over how sexual assault is handled on campuses across the country.

At Monday’s demonstration, students demanded an overhaul of the university’s sexual assault complaint process, the termination of certain school officials and stricter disciplinary action against alleged abusers.

In a statement to the student news outlet The Cornell Daily Sun, student organisers wrote that they were calling for the “abolition” of the Interfraternity Council system on campus and the “expulsion/revocation of degrees for all Chi Phi members involved in the rape”.

They also demanded that Cornell’s Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards be replaced by a “democratic disciplinary system”. Monday’s protest, they added, was designed to draw attention to the systemic failures that allow sexual violence to occur.

“We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the centre of Cornell’s administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual,” the students told the campus paper.

The alleged crime at the fraternity, they wrote, was part of a “rampant pattern of sexual assault perpetrated by members of Greek life at Cornell University and hundreds of other academic institutions throughout the country”.

Under pressure by New York Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James, the university announced this week it would be appointing a law firm to conduct an independent internal review of how it initially handled the case.

A transcript, obtained by US media, shows that although no charges were filed, Doe told campus police at the time that she could “say with 100% confidence I was raped”.

Her lawsuit also alleges that Cornell “afforded” the accused fraternity members “the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays” to the school. Two were later expelled, and another two were suspended.

articles.title: Scotland's first AI teacher warns pupils: Don't trust everything it tells you
articles.summary: Jamie Laycock says schools must help youngsters understand both the opportunities and dangers of AI.
articles.body:
Some teenagers are already using artificial intelligence to tackle homework, revise for exams and sharpen coursework.

Others are steering clear of it completely.

At one Scottish school, staff have decided that pretending AI doesn't exist is not an option.

Mearns Castle High School in East Renfrewshire is believed to be the first school in the UK to appoint a dedicated principal teacher of AI literacy, creating a role focused entirely on helping pupils and staff understand the risks and benefits of the powerful new technology.

The job has gone to Jamie Laycock, a former principal teacher of biology, who says schools must help youngsters understand both the opportunities and dangers of AI.

The message underpinning the new role is: "We can't just hope AI goes away".

But rather than teaching pupils to embrace AI, Laycock's mission is to ensure they can question it, challenge it and use it responsibly.

See if you can spot an AI deepfake with our test

In one of his first lessons, pupils were shown a mixture of real and AI-generated images and asked to spot the fakes.

Laycock says it's becoming increasingly difficult by the day, highlighting the rapid advances in so-called deepfakes.

But identifying fake images is only part of the course.

Laycock also teaches pupils about "hallucinations" where AI confidently provides information it has made up.

"I think hallucination is actually a really bad word, but it basically makes stuff up," he says.

"For a young person, if you don't have what we call 'foundational knowledge' it might be hard for you to figure out whether something is a hallucination or whether it's genuine."

He says young people need to be taught to be sceptical of any AI output and then go and check it to determine whether it is a genuine fact.

Another danger is "anthropomorphisation", where people treat chatbots like trusted friends or experts simply because they sound human.

"It has human-like qualities but actually this is just a machine," Laycock says.

"And for a young person, in particular, that is actually a really difficult thing to keep in perspective all the time."

Laycock also warns that AI often flatters users and agrees with them rather than challenging their ideas, creating risks for young people who may accept answers without thinking critically.

"It's sycophantic," he says. "It always tells you you're amazing, that your idea is great.

"We need to be teaching our young learners about that so that they don't get trapped and hooked into the technology and become over-reliant."

Another area pupils will be taught is AI's biases towards certain norms because of the information it is trained on.

The teacher says the lessons will be tailored to "different ages and stages" with younger pupils needing to be focused on foundational knowledge and critical thinking skills before moving on to practical uses of AI.

"We're not saying that we're advocates for AI, and we're not saying that it is good or bad," Laycock says.

"Our learners need to know how to use it appropriately so that they can get the best out of it.

"They need to be aware that this is a machine that they are interacting with, and for it certainly not to impact on their own ability to think and critically evaluate things."

Many schools in the UK have AI leads, teachers who take on some responsibility for AI alongside their day jobs, but this is thought to be the first time in the UK that a school has designated a specific role to AI literacy.

It follows a report by Edinburgh University published earlier this year which concluded that Scottish schools have not had the time nor capacity to prepare properly for the rapid rise in AI.

At Mearns Castle, all pupils in S1 and S2 will receive AI literacy lessons, while older year groups will cover the subject through citizenship and personal education (PSE) classes.

An elective course will also be available for senior pupils.

Laycock will also help to train colleagues on the use of AI and develop teaching materials which can be used by other schools.

The role was created after growing interest from both parents and pupils, many of whom are asking how AI will affect future careers.

A number of S6 pupils have volunteered to work with Laycock on how best to teach AI to the rest of the school.

Among them is 17-year-old Tomo, who had been planning to study finance and economics as he had always wanted to be a trader.

He now wonders whether AI could transform the profession before he even graduates.

"I think everybody's worried about what's going to be taken away by AI because we've got our university applications in the next few months," he says.

Fellow pupil Aydin said the technology should be used as a tool to aid understanding rather than provide easy answers.

"It shouldn't be used constantly," he says.

"It shouldn't be abused. I think it is always good to be as a little side help.

"It's better to use that for how to get to the answer, rather than just letting it do it for you and getting the straight answer there."

Another pupil, Anna, said the deepfake exercise left her less confident about her ability to distinguish real images from fake ones.

Head teacher Stuart Clark says it is clear that the implications of AI will be profound for the economy and on society.

"We're really clear that acting on AI is not the same thing as advocating for it or promoting it," he says.

"There will be risks associated with AI and there will be opportunities and it's really important that we don't make the same mistakes that society made with social media with young people adopting social media use without being fully educated on the implications."

The Scottish government published national guidelines on AI in March this year which highlight the importance of the ethical use of it, including not relying on it too much in educational settings and not allowing it to replace meaningful human interactions.

Education Secretary Màiri McAllan said: "It is encouraging to see schools and councils exploring how best to support AI literacy.

"As AI becomes more visible, it is important that learners and educators are supported to understand both the opportunities and challenges these technologies present.

"The guidance sets out principles to support local decision-making on the use of AI in education settings. Councils can use these principles to inform their approach to AI, taking account of their legal duties, existing arrangements and local circumstances."

She added: "AI, as a technology, is constantly developing at an exceptionally swift rate. As such, the Scottish government will keep matters under continual review."

articles.title: Rabbi who worked on Adam Brody's Netflix show slams actor over Gaza comments
articles.summary: Rabbi Steve Leder, who consulted on "Nobody Wants This," slammed show star Adam Brody for calling the situation in Gaza a genocide during a GQ interview.
articles.body: Adam Brody, who stars as Rabbi Noah Roklov in Netflix's "Nobody Wants This," recently made waves with his comments on the situation in Gaza, prompting criticism from a real-life rabbi who was a consultant on the show. When asked about his stance on Israel and Gaza in a recent interview with GQ, Brody said, "Put me down as thinking it's a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine. It's awful that it's taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it's reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago." Brody's remarks caught the attention of Rabbi Steve Leder, a Los Angeles-based rabbi who served as a consultant on the first season of "Nobody Wants this." Leder, who advised production on the show's portrayal of Judaism and Brody's role as a rabbi, posted a video to Instagram slamming the actor for his "flippant" remarks. "The flippancy was adding insult to injury, in my opinion, and needed to be addressed," Leder told Fox News Digital about why he posted the video to social media. "That is a word and that is a geopolitical situation that warrants anything but flippancy." 'NOBODY WANTS THIS' STAR ACCUSES ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' Leder emphasized that the word "genocide" has a specific definition and that Brody's use of it to describe what happened in Gaza was inaccurate. He quoted the United Nations' definition of genocide, which says the term is meant to describe a situation in which specific acts are carried out "with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group." "Israel's war is against Hamas. It is not against a nationality, it is not against an ethnicity, it is not a race, it is not against a religion," Leder told Fox News Digital. "There are many nationalities, ethnicities, races and religious people of various faiths living in Israel, comprising Israel's neighbors, and Israel has not and would not attack anyone for any of those reasons." The rabbi said that his main issue with Brody's remarks was that the actor presented his opinion as fact. "This is where I felt that Adam Brody went terribly wrong. He presented an opinion as a fact. And that is a mistake for any of us who are in the public eye," Leder said. In the show, Brody plays a rabbi who falls in love with an agnostic woman played by Kristen Bell, which is loosely based on the real-life romance between "Nobody Wants This" creator Erin Foster and her husband, Simon Tikhman. BILL MAHER RIPS MACKLEMORE'S GAZA STANCE, SAYS CELEBRITY 'MORAL CONFUSION' IS FUELING ANTISEMITISM Brody is far from the first Jewish celebrity to decry Israel's actions in Gaza as "genocide." Hannah Einbinder of "Hacks" and "Broad City" star Ilana Glazer have also been vocal critics of Israel. Leder told Fox News Digital that "they can say whatever they want as long as they acknowledge it's an opinion and not a fact." The rabbi explained that in Brody's case he felt compelled to respond because of the role he played in the production of "Nobody Wants This," which was deeply tied to Jewish representation on screen. Another element that added to the controversy over Brody's remarks is the fact that he plays a rabbi and has introduced many to Jewish culture through that role. Leder said it made the situation "doubly heartbreaking." MS RACHEL SAYS SHE WON’T WORK WITH ‘PRIVILEGED’ PEOPLE WHO STAY SILENT ON GAZA "Actors are not their roles, and we all understand that, they're acting. But in the minds of the public, in the mind of much of the pubic, it's sometimes hard to separate those two things," he said. "And when you have someone who is imagined — and I use that word deliberately — imagined to be an authority presenting opinions as facts, it's doubly painful." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Leder said public figures should stay away from discussing topics that they don't know enough about. In the video he released shortly after Brody's interview with GQ, Leder said, "If you know nothing about something, you should say nothing."

articles.title: World entering age of flux, India will rise to challenges: EAM S Jaishankar
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Stating that the world is entering an age of flux marked by uncertainties, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said he was confident that
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Stating that the world is entering an age of flux marked by uncertainties, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said he was confident that India will rise to the challenges at hand. "This is going to be an age of flux for the world, with conflicts and tariff volatility making it turbulent," said the minister, adding that responding to the challenges emerging out of the "choppy waters" is the main task.He was speaking at the 5th Kautilya Economic Conclave.Jaishankar, however, said that as India's record shows, "we have been able to rise to the challenges, whether it was Covid, or the challenge of a double conflict".Jaishankar also reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy was essential for resolving the Russia-Ukraine conflict."In July, there were attacks on civilian shipping by both Russia and Ukraine. And in the course of those attacks, some Indian sailors were killed. We regard these attacks as completely unacceptable. So, we protested to the Russians, to the Ukrainians. I took it up with the foreign ministers. We started getting active initially to secure the maritime shipping," he said. "So the conversation developed into whether non-attack on shipping is good, but is there a possibility of facilitating the shipment of grain... it got linked to energy. So, it became a broader conversation," he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Legislative privilege vs free speech: Supreme Court 7-judge bench may close case
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Nearly 23 years after it stayed the arrests of some journalists following the Tamil Nadu assembly passing a breach of privilege resolution
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Nearly 23 years after it stayed the arrests of some journalists following the Tamil Nadu assembly passing a breach of privilege resolution against them, the hearing scheduled before a seven-judge Supreme Court bench Wednesday, which promised to be a legal duel over the media's right to free speech versus the ambit of legislative privilege, appears to be an exercise for the records.For TN assembly, senior advocate Raju Ramachandran, flanked by attorney general R Venkataramani and solicitor general Tushar Mehta, told a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that the cause of action for the writ petition did not survive and the issue had become academic as the assembly withdrew the resolution imposing 15-day sentence on some journalists in 2004.A bench of CJI Kant and Justices Aravind Kumar, Prashant Kumar Mishra, Joymalya Bagchi, Vipul M Pancholi, Shree Chandrashekhar and V Mohana is scheduled to take up the petitions filed by N Ravi and S Selvam, then editors of 'The Hindu' and 'Murasoli' newspapers, respectively.Following the Nov 7, 2003, assembly resolution, arrest warrants were issued against the two editors and some journalists.CJI Kant said a seven-judge bench would assemble Tuesday, take the 2004 resolution on record and dispose of the petitions. articles.title: In a record, over 10,000 women clear JEE-Advanced
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Women's success rate in JEE-Advanced reached a record high in 2026 despite fewer registrations, with over 10,000 qualifying for the first time
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Women's success rate in JEE-Advanced reached a record high in 2026 despite fewer registrations, with over 10,000 qualifying for the first time during this period. Yet their share of IIT seat allotments barely changed, from 20.15% to 20.22%. Of the top 100 rankers, 97 were allotted seats at just three IITs - Bombay, Delhi and Madras - with Bombay alone taking 68.This time, a total 18,861 admissions were made in IITs, with 20% being female candidates. Among the top 25 rankers, 8 candidates each took admission in IIT Delhi and IIT Madras, while six toppers took admission in IIT Bombay.The Joint Implementation Committee report, prepared by IIT Roorkee, shows sharp gains for SC and ST candidates. Including candidates with disabilities in both years, their qualification rates among registered candidates rose by 9.9 and 8.3 percentage points, respectively, to 50.2% and 42.1%.SC qualifiers increased from 12,528 to 15,856, while the ST count rose from 5,017 to 6,379. Both increases were around 27%, faster than the 4.6% rise in the number of qualifiers, from 54,378 to 56,880.JEE(A): Women accountfor 23% of registrations but 17.8% of qualifiersOf 43,112 registered women, 10,107 qualified, taking their success rate to 23.4%, against 21.7% last year. In 2025, 9,404 women qualified from 43,413 registrations. Among women who appeared in both papers, the success rate was 24.9%.Women accounted for 23% of registrations but 17.8% of qualifiers, showing that their improved success rate has yet to close the gap with male candidates.Women received 3,814 seat allotments, up from 3,664, out of 18,861 overall. Their qualifying count grew 7.5%.IITs have added seats exclusively for women to ensure they make up at least one in five new undergraduate students. Their share of allotments is only slightly above that level. The report records 3,777 allotments in seats set aside for women and 37 in seats open to all genders. Women are considered first for women-only seats within the relevant category. The small number allotted seats open to all therefore does not show how many could have secured them on rank alone.The qualifying total also includes students eligible for a one-year preparatory course before starting an IIT degree. Their number rose from 9,644 to 13,127, nearly a quarter of all qualifiers. This route is available to eligible SC and ST candidates and those with disabilities against unfilled reserved seats. Those admitted must pass the course before entering allotted degree programme.Excluding this group, SC and ST qualifiers still increased by about 17% and 19%. However, the overall number qualifying directly for degree programmes fell from 44,734 to 43,753. The report records 189 seat allotments for this course. Qualifying for either of these routes does not guarantee an IIT seat; admission also depends on rank, eligibility and available seats.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: England’s lost medieval ‘Atlantis’ Shipden discovered beneath North Sea off Cromer; divers map 25 mysterious structures as new evidence challenges 700-year-old legend of St Peter’s Church
articles.summary: A medieval village that disappeared beneath the North Sea centuries ago is giving up new clues, but the most important piece of the puzzle remains missing.
articles.body: A medieval village that disappeared beneath the North Sea centuries ago is giving up new clues, but the most important piece of the puzzle remains missing.Divers investigating the remains of Shipden, a settlement off the coast of Cromer in Norfolk, have photographed and mapped 25 manmade features on the seabed, according to Popular Mechanics. Researchers are now trying to determine whether the underwater structures can finally establish the location of St. Peter’s Church, a building long associated with the vanished village.The search is also challenging a centuries-old local belief about a rocky formation known as Church Rock.A village lost to the seaShipden was once a thriving medieval coastal settlement. The Domesday Book of 1086 recorded 117 residents, three acres of meadow, 36 swine, a harbour, manor houses and two churches.The coastline looked very different at the time. Land that now lies beneath the North Sea once extended beyond the present-day cliffs around Cromer.Over several centuries, erosion, flooding, rising sea levels and powerful storms gradually consumed the settlement.The North Norfolk District Council has described Shipden as a “forgotten parish” swallowed by the sea and compared it with Norfolk’s own version of Atlantis.St. Peter’s Church became a legendShipden was associated with two settlements: Shipden-juxta-Mare, meaning Shipden by the sea, and Shipden-juxta-Felbrigg.St. Peter’s Church belonged to the coastal settlement. Historical records indicate that the church was damaged by the sea in 1317 and was underwater by about 1400.For centuries, local fishermen believed a formation known as Church Rock was actually the remains of St. Peter’s Church tower.According to the local legend, the church's bell could even be heard tolling beneath the waves.But researchers now believe that story may have been wrong.New underwater evidence challenges old beliefRecent seabed surveys suggest the church could have stood northwest of the traditional Church Rock location.That possibility means the flint formation long identified by local people as the church may instead be an unrelated underwater structure.Peter Stibbons, chairman of the Friends of Cromer Museum and a director of the project, told the BBC that the discovery represents a significant challenge to a story generations of Cromer residents grew up hearing.Researchers are currently comparing medieval documents with the physical evidence found underwater.Stibbons cautioned that the team is developing possible interpretations rather than presenting definitive conclusions.The North Sea changed Cromer’s coastlineThe disappearance of Shipden was not necessarily the result of one dramatic event.Historical evidence points to a combination of rising sea levels, severe storms, flooding and long-term coastal erosion.Sea levels reached particularly high levels around 1380, and by 1400 St. Peter’s Church had reportedly been submerged.Yet the church tower remained visible during very low tides for centuries, reportedly continuing into the 1800s.That visible remnant may have helped keep memories of the lost settlement alive.A 1888 accident may have added another layerThe mystery surrounding the underwater remains was further complicated in 1888, when the Great Yarmouth steam paddle tug Victoria struck a submerged obstruction while carrying passengers on an excursion to Cromer.The vessel became stuck, but everyone aboard was rescued by smaller boats.The obstruction was later destroyed using explosives.Researchers now believe that event could help explain some of the disturbed or toppled flintwork discovered by modern divers.It may also have influenced later local interpretations of what lay beneath the water.25 structures mapped beneath the seaThe investigation is part of the Alfred Savin Project, run by the Friends of Cromer Museum.Its objective extends beyond finding St. Peter’s Church. Researchers are studying how Cromer’s coastline changed over geological and historical timescales and how those changes affected settlements.Among the discoveries is a flint wall that may have been part of a medieval sea-defence structure, although researchers say further investigation is needed to establish its original purpose.The 25 mapped features provide new evidence of human activity in an area that is now completely underwater.The search will continueThe latest diving season has ended, with material and documentation collected during the investigation being taken to Cromer Museum for further examination.The precise location of St. Peter’s Church remains unresolved.For the researchers, however, finding the church is only part of the story. Each piece of masonry, historical document and seabed feature could help reconstruct a medieval landscape that disappeared beneath the North Sea.For now, Shipden remains one of England’s most intriguing lost settlements, a place where archaeology is slowly testing the boundary between historical fact and centuries-old coastal legend.You use AI every day. articles.title: Saudi Arabia urged to spare Sri Lankan sentenced to death over Facebook post
articles.summary: Anojan Sivarasa faces execution after he was found guilty of blasphemy over a Facebook comment.
articles.body:
"I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us."

Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi made a desperate plea for the life of her eldest son, Anojan Sivarasa. The 24-year-old migrant worker is facing the death penalty in Saudi Arabia after an appellate court found him guilty of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over a comment he made on Facebook.

The case has sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, sparking widespread concern and civil society petitions across the country. Multiple political parties and government bodies have co-ordinated diplomatic efforts seeking clemency.

However, the family has had no updates on his condition since 28 September. The Sri Lankan government has instructed the family to refrain from making further statements while diplomatic efforts take place.

Saudi authorities have not published an official execution timeline, and it remains unclear when the sentence will be carried out. Saudi Arabia has a history of carrying out executions without warning families or foreign embassies, only informing relatives after the sentence has been carried out.

Anojan was prosecuted after a dispute on social media following an incident that took place during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.

During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Anojan to post a response in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.

Although Anojan promptly deleted his comment and posted an apology video, it was screenshotted and brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.

His personal devices were subsequently seized, and his social media accounts were deleted by Saudi officials.

"People in Saudi Arabia knew nothing about this matter. It was individuals in Sri Lanka who sent emails to the company where my brother worked. I do not even wish to mention who those people are," Anojan's brother, Hamsidan Sivarasa, BBC Sinhala.

The company employing Anojan notified the authorities in Saudi Arabia who registered a case against him, according to Hamsidan.

Anojan was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of 3m Saudi riyals (about $0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. An appeal submitted on Anojan's behalf seeking to reduce his sentence was rejected, according to Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath.

The case took a drastic turn on 17 September after Saudi prosecutors filed an appeal for Anojan to be prosecuted under Sharia law instead of the country's cybercrime legislation. The appellate court granted the prosecution's request, increasing his sentence to the death penalty.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sri Lanka confirmed it is taking all available steps to assist Anojan.

His family met President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat on 21 September. The president assured them that the government would spare no effort to obtain a general pardon for him, instructing diplomatic channels to engage Saudi authorities.

The case has brought together cross-religious support. Senior Buddhist leaders, the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Nikaya and the Amarapura Maha Nikaya, together with Hindu religious leaders, handed over a memorandum to the Presidential Secretariat calling for urgent state intervention.

In addition, a four-member Sri Lankan legal delegation is travelling to Saudi Arabia this week to meet Anojan's local defence lawyers.

"There are two law firms in Saudi Arabia handling Anojan's case. We are going there to meet the lawyers from these two firms, discuss the case and plan what can be done next," one of the team, Upul Kumarapperuma, MP, told BBC Sinhala.

Back home, communication between Anojan and his family has completely ceased.

"My brother hasn't called for two days." Hamsidan said on 28 September. "We informed the embassy and asked officials to look into the matter and update us. They said they would check. We are still waiting, as we have not yet received a response."

In Saudi prisons, inmates on death row typically lose access to personal mobile devices, with formal calls strictly facilitated through prison authorities.

Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns regarding severe sentences for online speech in Saudi Arabia.

In July 2023, Mohammed Al Ghamdi, a retired Saudi school teacher, was sentenced to death over his comments on multiple social media platforms, according to the United Nations.

"The death sentence against Mohammad bin Nasser al-Ghamdi, who has a total of just 10 followers on both of his anonymous Twitter accounts and is accused of nothing other than expressing his opinions on social media, is ludicrous," Philip Luther, Amnesty International's Research and Advocacy Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said at the time.

Al Ghamdi's ruling was overturned, and he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to ALQST for human rights, an independent non-governmental organisation defending and promoting human rights in Saudi Arabia.

There are more than 10 million foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). Rights groups emphasise that low-wage migrant workers face distinct vulnerabilities in the Saudi legal system due to language barriers and lack of proper legal representation.

Executions for blasphemy are relatively rare compared with those for drug offences or murder handed down by courts in Saudi Arabia.
